items.title: Being mean to ChatGPT can boost its accuracy, but your tone could have an even bigger impact on computing costs
items.summary:
Bossing around an AI underling may yield better results than being polite, but that doesn’t mean a ruder tone won’t have consequences in the long run, researchers say.

A study from Penn State found ChatGPT’s 4o model produced better results on 50 multiple-choice questions as researchers’ prompts grew ruder.

Since then, Anthropic has moved to prohibit sustained cruelty toward its AI models, and the same researchers have found that prompt tone can also affect the computing resources AI consumes by as much as 44.3%.

In the original study from 2025, more than 250 unique prompts were sorted by politeness to rudeness, with the “very rude” response yielded an accuracy of 84.8%, four percentage points higher than the “very polite” response. Essentially, the LLM responded better when researchers gave it prompts like “Hey, gofer, figure this out,” than when they said “Would you be so kind as to solve the following question?”

While ruder responses generally yielded more accurate responses, the researchers noted “uncivil discourse” could have unintended consequences.

“Using insulting or demeaning language in human-AI interaction could have negative effects on user experience, accessibility, and inclusivity, and may contribute to harmful communication norms,” the researchers wrote at the time.

Chatbots read the room 

At the time it was published, the preprint study , which has not been peer-reviewed, offered new evidence that not only sentence structure, but tone, affects an AI chatbot’s responses—and that human’s interactions with AI may be more nuanced than they appeared on…
items.t: Being mean to ChatGPT can boost its accuracy, but your tone could have an even bigger impact on computing costs

items.title: Mark Cuban went 7 years without a vacation and Jeff Bezos worked 12-hour days. That kind of obsession is the secret to success, business coach says
items.summary:
While casual side hustles can sometimes pay off, the most successful people prioritize their passion to turn it into profit. 

Business coach and ex–Wall Streeter Codie Sanchez says all the successful people she’s met have one thing in common: “They’re obsessed.” 

“That’s it. That’s the secret,” says Sanchez, who has nearly 2 million TikTok followers and has interviewed nearly a dozen billionaires, including Palantir cofounder Joe Lonsdale . 

While all of the billionaires she’s interviewed on her podcast BigDeal are “wildly different,” she says in a video on her TikTok account that they’re all obsessed with what they do “almost to the point of it being uncomfortable.”

Sanchez actually got her start in journalism, winning the prestigious Robert F. Kennedy Journalism Award, before transitioning into finance, working for firms such as Vanguard, Goldman Sachs , and State Street . She’s the founder of Contrarian Thinking, a media and finance education company with millions of followers and subscribers, aimed at empowering people to take control of their financial future through unconventional paths like small-business ownership. She also runs venture fund Contrarian Thinking Capital, earned her MBA from Georgetown University, and is a New York Times bestselling author. Her estimated net worth is about $17 million.

Does obsession mean in entrepreneurship? 

One of the biggest debates in the workforce and entrepreneurship is whether work-life balance can really exist and whether it’s effective. 

If in fact, as Sanchez says, the most successful entrepreneurs and…
items.t: Mark Cuban went 7 years without a vacation and Jeff Bezos worked 12-hour days. That kind of obsession is the secret to success, business coach says

items.title: 2 years ago, Saudi Arabia quietly canceled the ‘petrodollar’ deal with America that wired the world economy for 50 years. Then war broke out in Iran
items.summary:
The gold standard may have ended in the early 1970s, but something else quietly took its place for the next 50 years: oil. 

The so-called  “petrodollar” system wasn’t well understood for most of this time, but a secret deal between Henry Kissinger and Saudi Arabia ensured the dollar would remain the dominant reserve currency. The ongoing war in Iran is exposing America’s Achilles’ heel, though, as China positions the “petroyuan” as the obvious successor, and to top it all off, the Saudis quietly killed the petrodollar two years ago. 

U.S. and Israel’s war on Iran has put a spotlight on the strength of the “petrodollar,” which makes up the cornerstone of America’s dominance over global trade, but economists warn the currency architecture has been eroding at its edges for years now.

Analysts are heralding the 2020s as marking the biggest change in the world’s relationship to the dollar since 1974, and every day the Iran war continues, the cracks in the old system grow wider and wider. To be sure, the dollar is still overwhelmingly dominant, but it’s no longer the only game in town. 

To understand this moment requires rewinding a bit to see how we got here.

What was Henry Kissinger’s secret trip ? 

In 1974, the U.S. negotiated a deal with Saudi Arabia in which the Gulf country agreed to sell oil in U.S. dollars alone . In return, the U.S. would provide military aid and security. The U.S., then under President Richard Nixon, was looking to secure global demand for the U.S. dollar following the end of the gold standard in 1971. In the wake of the 1973 oil crisis, the U.S.…
items.t: 2 years ago, Saudi Arabia quietly canceled the ‘petrodollar’ deal with America that wired the world economy for 50 years. Then war broke out in Iran

items.title: Vertex’s executive chairman: Here’s how we got our drug-trial success rate over 70% when the industry’s is 10% to 20%
items.summary:
Corporate America is locked in an innovation arms race – a race that is turning out very few winners. Companies are spending billions on R&D, acquisitions and new technologies, operating on the seemingly intuitive premise that making more bets is the best way to approach the uncertainty of the future.

But more bets don’t necessarily produce more successes.

There’s no more extreme example of this problem than pharmaceuticals and biotech. It takes an average of 10 to 15 years for a drug to go from the lab to regulatory approval. And more than 90% of drugs that enter clinical development fail. Just look at the headlines: one of the world’s largest pharmaceutical companies recently suffered three drug trial failures in a single week despite an enormous R&D budget, many talented scientists and a deep pipeline.

But this problem is far from unique to healthcare. In consumer tech, many startups flame out after a single hit; in automotive, EV pioneers are routinely outpaced by fast followers; digital investments in retail often fail to translate into customer growth.

The instinctive response when innovation fails is to do more of it: fund more projects, pursue more ideas, make more acquisitions and place more bets. If innovation is inherently unpredictable, the thinking goes, the best way to improve your chances of success is to increase the number of shots you take.

This kind of thinking is completely backward. It’s not about the shots. It’s about the target.

Imagine entering a darts tournament and throwing five consecutive bull’s-eyes, only to discover that you have been…
items.t: Vertex’s executive chairman: Here’s how we got our drug-trial success rate over 70% when the industry’s is 10% to 20%

items.title: Nvidia’s next CEO must lead a supervised international business—amid the ‘complete reorganization of the AI equilibrium,’ investor says
items.summary:
Following the ouster of Jensen Huang as Nvidia CEO, the company’s next chief executive will inherit a company facing a fundamentally different set of challenges than the ones that once propelled it to become the world’s most valuable company. 

Beyond sustaining demand for its AI chips, the next leader needs to navigate intensifying U.S. export restrictions, investigations into the company’s China business and scrutiny of its financial arrangements.

That’s according to Nvidia investor Bill Birmingham, managing director at REX Financial—the parent company of REX Shares, which oversees $8.5 billion in assets under management.

“The bigger problem going forward isn’t actually who sits in the CEO chair. It is the Chinese chip access,” he told Fortune via email. 

For years, U.S. restrictions sought to limit China’s ability to purchase Nvidia’s most powerful processors. But Huang’s affair with an executive at Singapore-based tech company Megaspeed raised concerns about Chinese companies accessing restricted hardware.

The Trump administration is now moving to plug those gaps. Last Sunday, the federal government announced a rule to close a loophole that allowed remote access to advanced AI chips and servers via overseas data centers. And on Friday, President Donald Trump said he wanted to prevent American companies from building data centers overseas.

“Whoever runs Nvidia next will inherit a narrower, more closely supervised international business and the complete reorganization of the AI equilibrium that comes with it,” Birmingham said.

items.title: I am SNL’s ‘sister.’ caregiving is an act of love, but love isn’t a care plan
items.summary:
The Saturday Night Live ’s “Sister” sketch struck a chord with families across the nation. Why? Because they saw themselves in the story. Let’s face it: when an aging parent needs care, it’s often the women, the “Sisters”, who step up and take on the responsibility. 

I’m grateful to SNL for bringing this topic forward. Sometimes humor opens the door to a conversation we have been avoiding. But recognizing the problem is only the beginning. We have to change what we expect from the women in our families.

For me, watching the video was painful and hit very close to home. And the many texts I received afterward, as CEO of A Place for Mom, were even more heartbreaking. I am the sister. I know firsthand what that responsibility feels like because my mom and I cared for my incredible grandparents for nearly 20 years. 

I came to the United States as a teenager and helped my grandparents navigate senior care while still learning the system myself. I know what it means to feel tremendous guilt, worry about people you love, and not know where to turn.

For 25 years, we have been helping families navigate one of life’s most difficult and emotional journeys: finding care for an aging loved one. More than 2.3 million families have turned to us for support, and approximately 40% of family caregivers we serve are daughters, daughter-in-laws, nieces and sisters-in-law. In fact, more than two-thirds of the people that reach out are women. 

Once we connect with the family, our goal is to help them understand where to start, make sense of their options, navigate difficult decisions, and…
items.t: I am SNL’s ‘sister.’ caregiving is an act of love, but love isn’t a care plan

items.title: Americans are paying $290 to meet strangers as friendship apps spread to more than 200 cities
items.summary:
Startups are betting on America’s loneliness epidemic, and Americans are buying in. Apps such as 222, Real Roots, and Timeleft are turning friend-matching events into a growing consumer market, and some users pay hundreds of dollars to make new friends offline.

Alexandra Pitzer paid $290 through Real Roots last year to meet a group of strangers, The New York Times reported . She had just moved from Nashville to Honolulu for her husband’s Army job and was looking for connection. The app placed her at a brewery with eight other women.

“I can see most of them being lifelong friends,” Pitzer told the Times . “We have a genuine connection.”

The business is working, at least for now: each of the three companies brings in millions of dollars in revenue a year, according to the Times . But the model carries an unusual tension. The better it works, the less its customers may need it.

How 222 turned backyard dinners into a venture-backed startup 

These companies are tapping into demand for in-person connection at a time when many people struggle to build relationships in a digital age. Rather than meeting people the old-fashioned way, users are matched with strangers based on shared interests and personality, then sent to curated events.

222 began as a college research project. Its co-founders later started hosting dinners in their backyard, and the project became a full-time business in 2023, according to the Times .

The company has since raised $13.7 million in venture capital, according to Business Insider , including $10.1 million in 2025. It uses machine-learning models…
items.t: Americans are paying $290 to meet strangers as friendship apps spread to more than 200 cities

items.title: ‘I don’t blame any woman for being sucked in’: how the wellness industry is cynically exploiting menopause

‘Tequila?” says a woman brightly, proffering a pink plastic shot glass. It’s barely 10.30 on a Saturday morning, and my perimenopause wellness journey is not going entirely as expected. We are standing in a neon-lit London conference centre amid the hubbub of Pause Live, billed as the UK’s biggest annual women’s health and menopause event and essentially a consumer fair for those in midlife. All around me, women are sampling free squirts of menthol lotion (supposed to cool hot flushes) and paper thimblefuls of slightly grainy, sweet latte made with powdered Peruvian maca root instead of coffee.

The tequila, it turns out, is a gift from the sponsors, with no miracle ingredients beyond alcohol. But stalls offer everything from neck creams to pelvic-floor trainers, mindfulness journals and hairpieces for disguising thinning locks, plus herbal supplements in every conceivable edible form: chocolate truffles, ginger shots, mushroom coffee. items.t: ‘I don’t blame any woman for being sucked in’: how the wellness industry is cynically exploiting menopause

items.title: Trump’s USDA changed the rules. Farmers and rural businesses paid the price
items.summary:
This year, I was forced to lay off all five of my employees. My business wasn’t defeated by a competitor or a declining market. It was devastated by a decision from my own government.

I founded Sun Grants Consulting in 2023 to help farmers and rural small businesses apply for grants through the Rural Energy for America Program (REAP). We grew to five employees and filed almost 200 applications.

In March, USDA announced it would stop processing pending REAP applications and make no further grant awards until new regulations took effect. Applicants who had followed the existing rules would have to start over . Fifty-seven of my clients’ applications were caught in that decision, representing more than $22 million in rural energy investments and more than $9 million in grant awards. Because my firm is paid only when clients win grants, our anticipated revenue from those applications vanished.

Congress created REAP in the 2002 farm bill to encourage renewable energy and efficiency investments. It has enjoyed bipartisan support, including reauthorization in the 2018 farm bill President Trump signed. REAP is not a blank check: Farmers and business owners put their own capital at risk, hire private contractors and pay costs the grants do not cover.

Then came a second blow. USDA issued a new rule in October that fundamentally changed how future applicants qualify. Farmers and businesses generally must complete projects, pay the bills and document 12 months of energy production or savings before they can even apply. items.t: Trump’s USDA changed the rules. Farmers and rural businesses paid the price

items.title: $3 billion Remote CEO told every employee to take a five-hour AI course or miss expectations in their performance review: ‘Get with the times’
items.summary:
With AI coming for jobs, the $3 billion HR platform Remote is forcing its workers to get ahead of it. Employees get five hours of paid company time to take the course. But there’s a catch: skip it and you can forget about a passing performance review.

It’s all part of CEO Job van der Voort’s push to get Remote’s roughly 2,000 employees up to speed on AI.

“AI will run the world so it’s about getting with the times,” van der Voort told Fortune . In his view, employers should get their workers up to scratch—so he launched the free AI crash course, aiforactualwork.com , and made the first course mandatory for his entire workforce.

“It’s very important for companies to take responsibility. They are our people. We hired them. We decided, and then we said to them, ‘the bar now is that you start using AI,’ so yes, we should totally take responsibility for the people that work for us,” he added. 

“If you are a company that employs a whole bunch of people, you should take responsibility for the people that work for you. You’re not going to be able to fire all the people that work for you and find new people that are good with this.”

But responsibility goes both ways. Staff who didn’t take him up on the offer would face consequences. “We became really clear. What we said is you have to do it, and if you don’t, you’re not going to get ‘meeting expectations’ in your performance review,” van der Voort said. “So everybody did it.”

Luckily, the threat alone worked, and now everyone in his company is up to speed. 

“It just raises the foundational level that we can expect everybody…
items.t: $3 billion Remote CEO told every employee to take a five-hour AI course or miss expectations in their performance review: ‘Get with the times’

items.title: Elon Musk’s SpaceX is betting $74 billion on AI data centers. Texas and Arizona want to know who pays for the power
items.summary:
SpaceX wants to build a data center in the Arizona desert that would draw 6,000 megawatts of power at full build-out. That is nearly two-thirds of the all-time peak demand that Arizona Public Service, which serves about 1.5 million homes and businesses, hit across its entire system this summer, according to KJZZ .

The Cochise County campus is the larger half of a plan SpaceX announced on Nov. 12 to spend more than $74 billion on two AI supercomputing sites: roughly $50 billion in southeastern Arizona and more than $24 billion at Starbase, Texas, Reuters reported . The company is pitching both as projects that pay for themselves, with on-site power in Texas, dry cooling in Arizona, and promises of lower bills and taxes for neighbors.

Residents, local officials, and now Arizona’s attorney general want proof first. Who covers the cost of the power plants, water, and grid upgrades behind AI, the company or the people who live next door, is quickly becoming the question that decides whether these campuses get built.

The stakes for SpaceX are large. Its AI segment produced more than half of its third-quarter revenue, ahead of rockets and Starlink, according to Reuters, and Fortune has reported on how renting out computing capacity to Anthropic and Google has become central to the company’s valuation. The political ground is shifting under the industry, too: voters sided against data center development in 37 of 38 local ballot contests with complete counts this month, as Fortune reported after the midterms .

In Texas, a land swap puts the project past a moratorium 

The Texas…
items.t: Elon Musk’s SpaceX is betting $74 billion on AI data centers. Texas and Arizona want to know who pays for the power

items.title: A truism for our political leaders: until work again involves respect and decent levels of pay, this crisis will continue | John Harris
items.summary:
Last week’s Milburn review contained telling phrases, but the core problem is not Neets: it’s what capitalism as we know it has done to employment

Everyday pride and contentment. That’s what work should give us. In 15-plus years of speaking to ordinary people and politicians about the UK’s serial woes and crises, one thing has revealed itself to me time and time again: the mess of cant, contradictions and tensions in our national understanding of work. Indeed, the higher up the hierarchies of power and influence any conversation about work goes, the more one vitally important subject seems to fall away: what paid employment actually is or ought to be.

All of this is reflective of a very British kind of amnesia. Of course poorly rewarded, unreliable jobs have always been part of our economy – and in the past a focus of fierce social conflict. But well within living memory a combination of the power of trade unions and the collective social conscience built into the postwar consensus resulted in an economy and labour market that now seem almost inconceivable. For sure they were scattered with restrictive practices and base prejudice: fathers securing jobs for their sons, people from minorities being excluded from work not just by people in management but by their fellow workers, and a great deal of…

items.title: I hated life as a Neet. But now I’ve found a job, life is just as precarious | Emilija Morrison
items.summary:
The government’s plans to help young people not in education, work or training are welcome – I dearly hope they offer long-term security

  • Emilija Morrison is a University of Glasgow graduate and holds a Gold Standard NCTJ Diploma in journalism

What child dreams of being unemployed when they grow up? You can probably remember the days, aged 10, when you were asked to present to the class what you wanted to be. Imagine hearing this: “I want to be unemployed. After I graduate from university, I want to go to the jobcentre in my home town and collect my benefits every month.”

Yet that is the reality for many young people today – childhood dreams to become a teacher, a doctor, an engineer or whatever other profession thwarted not by the limits of their abilities, but the reality of the economy.

items.title: The Guardian view on Britain and Europe: Burnham’s reset cannot be the final destination | Editorial
items.summary:
It’s welcome news that Labour has reopened doors that the Conservatives slammed shut. But the fundamental dilemma over European integration remains

Andy Burnham on Friday announced a long-awaited deal to ease some of Brexit’s barriers. But EU sources say the agreements, or at least some of them, won’t take effect until Britain has resolved a dispute over its demand for European students to pay the same university tuition fees as British ones. The prime minister had hoped to turn the page on Brexit’s endless haggling. Instead, he was reminded that closer ties come at a price. This does not negate his achievement. The deals ease trade barriers on food, shield British exporters from EU carbon tariffs and let up to 100,000 young people on each side live and work across the Channel for three years. But Mr Burnham cannot claim an unqualified diplomatic victory.

Clearly, such an advance would have been unimaginable under the Conservatives or Reform. The Tories say they will rip up the agreements, though that stance carries the risk of alienating voters lost to the Liberal Democrats in 2024. Nigel Farage
